The email came at 4:10, while Rania was still in her school uniform at the kitchen table in their Sydney flat. Selective school test: not offered a place.
She read it three times. Then she closed the laptop very gently, as if it might break.
Mum had worked Saturday shifts at the bakery all year to pay for the Tuesday tutoring. Dad had stuck the practice timetable on the fridge. Her little cousins in Beirut had been told she was 'the clever one'.
Not clever, she thought. Just the one who costs them money. Every Saturday, for nothing.
Jin messaged: 'did u get yours??' She turned the phone face down.
When Mum came home and asked, Rania said she had a headache and went to her room. She lay there listening to her parents' voices in the kitchen and decided she was simply the stupid one in the family. That was the whole story now.

qa.q: Who had worked Saturday shifts at the bakery to pay for tutoring?
qa.a: Rania's Mum had worked Saturday shifts at the bakery all year.

qa.q: What does Rania's thought 'Just the one who costs them money' show about how she sees herself?
qa.a: She has turned one failed test into a verdict on her whole self, feeling ashamed and like a burden on her parents.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Rania at this stage?
qa.a: She could tell her Mum or a school counsellor what she is really thinking, so someone can help her see that one result does not decide who she is.

qa.q: How might Rania's Mum feel hearing that her daughter has 'a headache' and seeing her go straight to her room?
qa.a: Mum may sense something is wrong and feel worried and shut out, not knowing Rania thinks the tutoring money was wasted on her.

grounding: It shows a teenager who failed an entrance test deciding she is stupid and a cost to her family, turning one result into a verdict on herself.

The results sheet was pinned outside the coaching centre's office, and by six the corridor was packed. Nandini found her roll number and ran her finger along the row twice. Below cut-off. Well below.
Sunaina, her roommate from the hostel, found her on the staircase landing, sitting with her bag on her knees.
'Nandu? What did you get?'
Nandini didn't look up. 'Papa took a loan for this place, you know that? Two years' fees. And Ma tells everyone at the temple that I'll be the first engineer in the family.' She laughed, but it came out wrong. 'I'm the dumb one. I've always been the dumb one. I just made them pay to find out.'
Sunaina sat down beside her. The fan above them creaked. Down the corridor someone was cheering.
'I can't even call home,' Nandini said. 'What would I say? Sorry I'm a waste?'

I'm Vandana, Payal's didi. I can only tell you what I saw that week.
On Monday Payal came home from school and went straight to the bathroom for a long time. At dinner Mummy asked if the physics unit test papers were back. Payal said, 'Not yet, Ma'am is very slow.'
On Tuesday I saw a folded answer sheet sticking out of the side pocket of her bag. Red ink. I didn't open it.

Maybe it was. I don't know. But she hasn't opened her physics notebook all week, and she used to love that subject.

The parent-teacher meeting ran late, and Mohit sir was on his fourteenth family when Divyansh's father sat down, Divyansh standing stiffly behind him.
The mid-term report lay open: 41 in science.
'His cousin Saurabh got 92,' the father said, before Mohit sir could speak. 'Same school, same books. Our neighbour's son also. Only this one is like this.'
Divyansh stared at a crack in the classroom floor. His ears had gone red.
Mohit sir answered the father's questions politely. When the father stepped out to take a phone call, the teacher turned to Divyansh and said quietly, 'One result is a result. It isn't you. I've seen your lab work.'
Divyansh looked up, startled.
'Come to the staff room on Monday, after lunch. We'll look at what went wrong in the paper and make a plan for three weeks. Just us.'
Divyansh nodded once.

qa.a: Divyansh got 41 in science on the mid-term report.

passage:
When our tiffin service shut down in my final year, I learned there are many ways people can make you feel worse while trying to help.
My mausi hugged me and said, 'Poor boy, all that effort.' My uncle at a wedding told me I should have done an MBA first, then a business. Someone else mentioned, twice, that my cousin in Pune had just been promoted.
I nodded at all of it. I went home each time feeling smaller.
Hafsa was different. She'd been our first customer. She found me on the library steps a week later and just sat down. 'Tell me what happened,' she said. So I did, all of it, the supplier, the price, the last day. She didn't fix anything. She said, 'That sounds really hard, Nitin.' That was it.
A month later I walked into the placement office for the first time. I think those two hours on the steps are why.

qa.q: Where did Hafsa find Nitin a week after the shutdown?
qa.a: She found him on the library steps.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel after the pity, advice and comparisons from relatives?
qa.a: He felt smaller each time, as if their help pointed out his failure instead of easing it.

qa.q: What did Hafsa's way of helping get right?
qa.a: She listened without judging or fixing, and named how hard it was, which helped Nitin feel steady enough to move forward.

qa.q: How might Nitin's mausi see her own words if she read this account?
qa.a: She might be surprised, since she meant to be kind, and realise that pity made him feel worse rather than supported.

grounding: It shows a young man whose venture failed receiving pity, advice and comparison from relatives, and being helped most by a friend who just listened.

Counsellor's note, college wellness room. Written by Farida.
Nandini (20) came in on Thursday, two weeks after her CA intermediate results. She said she had failed both groups. She sat with her dupatta twisted round one hand and said she'd come because 'everyone keeps talking at me'.
She listed it quite flatly: her aunt cried and called her 'bechari'; her father forwarded her articles on 'how toppers study'; a neighbour asked, in front of her, whether her cousin had cleared on the first try.
'I know they love me,' she said. 'I just feel like a project now.'
I didn't offer tips. I asked what the last two weeks had been like and let her talk. Near the end she cried, then laughed at herself, and her shoulders dropped.
Next: she has asked to come again next Thursday. I will keep the session for listening unless she asks for planning.

qa.a: She came in two weeks after her CA intermediate results.

qa.q: What does Nandini mean when she says 'I just feel like a project now'?
qa.a: She feels that her family's pity and advice treat her as something to fix, which leaves her feeling judged rather than loved.

qa.q: Which choice by Farida helped Nandini, and why?
qa.a: Farida gave no tips and let her talk, and that non-judging space let Nandini cry, relax and want to come back.

qa.q: How might Nandini's father see his forwarded articles differently after hearing how she felt?
qa.a: He might understand that his well-meant advice added pressure, and that simply listening could help her more.

grounding: It shows a young woman after a failed exam receiving pity, advice and comparison, and a counsellor whose non-judging listening helps her start to recover.

14 June, night.
Madhav's selection letter came today. He called me first, before his own parents. I said 'Congratulations, yaar!' and meant it, and then I went on the terrace and felt sick with envy. We did the same runs at 5 a.m. for two years. Same books. He's going to the academy and I'm going to... I don't know where.

Chachu told me today, 'Everything happens for a reason, beta, something better is coming.' Maybe. But I don't want a better story yet. I want to be allowed to be sad about this one for a bit.

I'll deal with the next plan next week.

Sunday, two weeks after. Nikita still couldn't say the words 'the shop closed' without her throat tightening. When Tanuja asked, she said, 'I was useless. I did everything wrong.' A minute later: 'Actually, the courier rates went up, it's not my fault.' Both felt true and neither helped.
Wednesday. Tanuja came over with a notebook and drew three columns: in my control, luck, change next time. Nikita filled them slowly. In control: she never raised prices, and she stopped posting new plants in the monsoon. Luck: the courier rates, the heavy rain in August. Change: price for delivery, keep a small stock, check the numbers monthly. She crossed out 'useless'. It didn't fit any column.
The next Saturday she showed the page to her old supplier, who nodded at the price column and said, 'Yes. That was it.' Nikita felt oddly lighter.

qa.q: What three columns did Tanuja draw?
qa.a: She drew three columns: in my control, luck, change next time.

Sit down, Eshaan. Your Chinmay Chacha has lost more than one pitch, you know.
When I was twenty-four I failed the state services prelims. I didn't leave my room for three days. Then, for weeks, I swung between two stories. Story one: I'm just not smart enough. Story two: the paper was unfair, the questions changed, bad luck.
My old teacher, Joshi-ma'am, made me write a list. Three questions. What was in my hands? I never did full mock tests with a timer. I read, but I didn't practise. What was luck? Yes, the pattern changed that year. Everyone got the same luck, though. What would I change? Timed tests, every Sunday.
That list was the most useful thing I wrote that whole year, Eshaan. Not because it made me feel better. Because it told me what to do.
So. Your pitch. Get a paper.

passage:
After the café in São Paulo closed, Priscila didn't bake for two months. Just looking at the mixer made her tired.
In March her friend Jana said her aunt had a free corner at the Saturday street market in Pinheiros. 'One table. One kind of cake. That's all.'
Priscila made twelve orange cakes. She sold nine, and gave three to the fruit seller next door, who came back and bought two more for his daughter's birthday.
The next Saturday she made fifteen and sold out by eleven. The third week a woman asked if she took orders for parties. Priscila wrote her number on a napkin, her hand a little shaky.
She still woke some nights thinking about the café. But on Friday evenings now she was measuring flour again, humming, and on the way home from the market she started, without meaning to, making a list of new flavours.

qa.q: How many orange cakes did Priscila make for the first Saturday?
qa.a: She made twelve orange cakes.

qa.q: What does Priscila's humming on Friday evenings suggest about how she is feeling?
qa.a: It suggests her confidence and enjoyment are slowly returning as the small weekly successes build up 🙂

qa.q: Why did starting with one table and one kind of cake work well for Priscila?
qa.a: It was small enough to manage after a big failure, so each sold-out Saturday gave her a real win that rebuilt confidence through doing.

qa.q: How does Jana probably feel watching Priscila make lists of new flavours?
qa.a: Jana is likely relieved and proud, glad that the small idea Jana suggested helped Priscila bake again.

grounding: It shows a person restarting at a small scale after a failure, collecting small wins, and regaining confidence through action rather than thought.

The community centre's evening study room smelled of chalk and mosquito coil. Reena arrived at six every Tuesday and Thursday, a month after failing the teacher eligibility test for the second time.
Yusuf, who ran the centre, had given her two Class 6 students and one corner blackboard. 'Just fractions,' he'd said. 'Nothing grand.'

Kishore found Ujjwal in the office canteen in Hyderabad, holding a tea he wasn't drinking. 'The client cancelled,' Kishore said. 'Six months of work. I keep thinking I'm finished here.'
Ujjwal pulled out a chair for him. 'Sit. Did I ever tell you about my first company?'
Kishore shook his head.
'At twenty-one, two friends and I started a bike-repair app. Took money from my father. Shut down in eight months. I didn't answer my phone for a week.'
He said it plainly, the way you'd describe a train you missed.
'It was the worst year I've had. It also taught me I like building things with people more than I like being the boss. And that I can survive a big failure.' He shrugged. 'You'll survive this one. Tomorrow, let's list what the client actually said. Then we decide what's next.'
Kishore finally drank his tea.

qa.q: How long did Ujjwal's first company last before it shut down?
qa.a: It shut down in eight months.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when he said 'I keep thinking I'm finished here'?
qa.a: He felt crushed and afraid that one cancelled project meant the end of his career at the company.

qa.q: What made Ujjwal's way of supporting Kishore effective?
qa.a: He shared his own failure plainly, showed what it had taught him, and offered a concrete next step, so Kishore felt less alone and less hopeless.

qa.q: How might Kishore see Ujjwal differently after this conversation?
qa.a: Kishore may see him not as someone who always succeeded but as someone who failed and rebuilt, which makes his own situation seem survivable.

grounding: It shows a person who can now speak plainly of an old failure as a chapter that taught resilience and clarified values, and who uses it to support someone else.

passage:
My first three months on the support team in Bengaluru, I was always the last one out. The cleaner, Selvi akka, used to switch off the lights around me.
I told myself I was being dedicated. Really, I was hiding. Everyone else seemed to know what 'escalation matrix' meant, what 'P1' meant, how to read the logs. I didn't. Shalini, my senior, sat two desks away and kept saying, 'Ask me anything, Siami.' I never did. Asking felt like showing everyone I didn't belong.
So I stayed back and read old tickets. At home I watched tutorial videos till one, and came in with red eyes.
It took me three weeks to figure out, alone, something Shalini explained to another new joiner in five minutes. I heard it from my desk. That was the first time I thought, Lalremsiami, what are you doing?

qa.q: What did Shalini keep saying to Lalremsiami?
qa.a: Shalini kept saying, 'Ask me anything, Siami.'

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami never ask Shalini for help?
qa.a: Asking felt like proving to everyone that Siami didn't belong, so staying quiet felt safer than exposing gaps.

qa.q: What went wrong with Lalremsiami's way of catching up, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Studying alone at night and never asking cost weeks and sleep; asking Shalini even a few questions a day would have been much faster.

qa.q: How might Shalini have seen the new joiner who stayed late but never asked anything?
qa.a: Shalini may have wondered whether the offer wasn't trusted, or thought Siami was coping fine and didn't need help.

grounding: It shows a new hire staying late, not asking questions and studying at night to catch up, because hiding gaps feels safer, which slows learning.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Supervisor's note: new joiner check-in. Written by Ayesha, payroll team.
Keerthana (22) joined six weeks ago. Her work is accurate. But the security log shows her badge out after 9 p.m. on most days, and she arrives before anyone else.
In our team meetings she has not asked a single question. When I explain a new process, she nods and writes. Yesterday I found a page she'd left on the printer: a list of terms we use, 'arrears', 'LOP', 'full and final', each with notes copied from the internet, some of them wrong.
When I asked how she was finding things, she said, 'All fine, ma'am, I'm just a bit slow, I'm catching up at home.' She looked tired.
Next step: I've set a ten-minute slot every morning this week where she brings three questions, any questions. I'll tell her I did the same when I joined.

qa.q: What did Ayesha find on the printer?
qa.a: She found a list of terms like 'arrears', 'LOP' and 'full and final', with notes copied from the internet, some of them wrong.

qa.q: What might Keerthana be worried about when she says she is 'just a bit slow'?
qa.a: She may fear that asking questions will show she doesn't know enough, so she works late to hide it.

qa.q: How could Ayesha's daily ten-minute question slot help Keerthana?
qa.a: It makes asking normal and safe, so Keerthana can clear doubts quickly instead of learning slowly and wrongly on her own.

qa.q: How does Keerthana's pattern look from Ayesha's side as a supervisor?
qa.a: Ayesha sees accurate work but a tired new joiner learning some things wrongly in secret, and feels she needs to step in gently.

grounding: It shows a new hire staying late, avoiding questions and studying at home to catch up, and a supervisor noticing how this slows her learning.
